37923.explanation: A panegyric is a formal or elaborate piece of writing or poem written to praise or glorify a person, thing or event. While an ode is also a poem of praise, it is more meditative and lyrical in nature, whereas the direct aim of a panegyric is to praise or admire the subject of the poem.

And, the setting includes the time and place where the drama unfolds, providing context for the characters and action.

37930.question_text:

The pattering rain was kicking up little
explosions of dust in the glade.He heard the
faint whisper of the stream as it stole across
the land and disappeared into the bush.

The figure of speech underlined in line 1 is
37930.explanation:
Onomatopoeia refers to words that imitate or resemble the sound they describe. These words are often used in literature and everyday language to create a vivid auditory effect. Examples include "buzz" (like a bee), "bang" (like a loud noise), "sizzle" (like food cooking), and "meow" (the sound a cat makes). 

"pattering" is an onomatopoeic word used to imitate the sound of rain.

37931.subject: Literature in English
37931.question_text: In poetry, rhythm is a regular pattern of
37931.explanation: In poetry, rhythm refers to the pattern of sounds and beats created by the arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables.  For example, the iambic pentameter, commonly used in English poetry, consists of five feet per line, each foot containing an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable (da-DUM). This creates a rhythmic structure that is pleasing to the ear and helps convey the poem's meaning.

37933.question_text: In a play, a long speech by a single character in the presence of other characters is called
37933.explanation:
In a play, a long speech by a single character in the presence of other characters is called:

B. monologue

A monologue is a speech delivered by one character, and it is typically addressed to other characters on stage or to the audience. This is different from a soliloquy, which is a speech where a character speaks their thoughts aloud when alone on stage. An aside is a brief remark made by a character to the audience, unheard by other characters on stage. A prologue, on the other hand, is an introductory section of a play or literary work.

  • plot

  • characters

  • setting

  • theme

The main difference is length and scope:

  • A novel is longer and more detailed.

  • A short story is shorter and more compact.

38123.subject: Literature in English
38123.explanation:
In The Marriage of Anansewa by Efua Sutherland, Ananse is the central character known for his cunning and manipulative behaviour. In the passage, Speaker A excitedly says, “Delicious news… Sweet news Mr. Honourable… Did he specify the day?” and even calls for drinks to celebrate. This tone of excitement and calculation fits Ananse’s character, especially when he is scheming about his daughter’s marriage arrangements for financial gain.

The reference to “Mr Honourable” also suggests he is speaking to a messenger or intermediary bringing him information — something Ananse frequently does in the play.

38125.question_text:

Occupies my thoughts. How can I ever forget that
you have done me great honour? To show my
gratitude. I will guard the object of your interest....
with all the vigilance in my power......

The speaker is
38125.explanation: The passage reflects a tone of gratitude and cleverness, which is characteristic of Ananse, the famous West African trickster spider. The speaker talks about being honoured and promising to guard an object of interest with vigilance, which is Ananse, who strategically navigates situations to his advantage.

38130.subject: Literature in English
38130.explanation: Speaker B is Ananse. He is witty, cunning and exaggerates or flatters to achieve his aims, particularly regarding marriage arrangements and presenting suitors.

38131.subject: Literature in English
38131.explanation: Speaker A is Anansewa, the daughter while Speaker B is Ananse, her father. In the first part of the dialogue, Anansewa is protesting. She is a modern girl (attending secretarial school) and is horrified by the idea of being given away to a "chief with fifty wives." Her father, Ananse, uses his "cunning" to manipulate her perspective. He knows his daughter is vain and romantic, so he stops describing the suitors as "old chiefs" and starts describing them as handsome, powerful, and "glowing black."
